claims.text: Catalytic activity of transition-metal catalysts is governed by the oxidation state of the metal center.
The metal-center oxidation state influences adsorption and desorption of reactants and products.
Oxidation-state-dependent adsorption and desorption affect catalytic selectivity and durability.
The relevant structural mediators are metal-ligand interactions and coordination geometry.
Changing the metal-center oxidation state modulates the catalyst's electronic properties.
Changes in catalyst electronic properties alter reactant and product adsorption and desorption.
Adsorption and desorption changes alter catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
Varying oxidation state will produce a 20% increase in catalytic activity relative to a catalyst with a fixed oxidation state.
Varying oxidation state will produce a 15% improvement in selectivity relative to a catalyst with a fixed oxidation state.
Activity and selectivity changes can be measured through reaction rates and product yields.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to oxidation states from +2 to +4, temperatures from 250°C to 350°C, and pressures from 1 atm to 5 atm.
Support effects, particle size, and morphology may influence the relationship between oxidation state and catalytic activity.
Failure of activity and selectivity to change by more than 5% when oxidation state changes would falsify the hypothesis.
